content: Chromium is a chemical element represented by the symbol Cr and has an atomic number of 24. It is a steel-gray, lustrous, and hard metal that can achieve a high polish and has a high melting point. Chromium is odorless, tasteless, and malleable. On July 26, 1761, Johann Gottlob Lehmann discovered an orange-red mineral in the Ural Mountains, which he named Siberian red lead. Although initially misidentified as a lead compound containing selenium and iron, the material was actually lead chromate (PbCrO4), now known as the mineral crocoite. In 1770, Peter Simon Pallas visited the same site and identified a red lead mineral with useful properties as a pigment for paints. The use of Siberian red lead as a paint pigment quickly gained popularity, and a bright yellow pigment derived from crocoite became fashionable. In 1797, Louis Nicolas Vauquelin obtained samples of crocoite ore and successfully produced chromium oxide (CrO3) by reacting crocoite with hydrochloric acid. By 1798, Vauquelin isolated metallic chromium by heating the oxide in a charcoal oven. He also detected traces of chromium in precious gemstones such as rubies and emeralds. Later that year, he successfully isolated chromium atoms. During the 1800s, chromium was primarily used in paints and tanning salts. Today, 85% of chromium usage is in metal alloys, with the remainder used in the chemical, refractory, and foundry industries. The name chromium is derived from the Greek word chrôma, meaning color, due to the many colorful compounds it forms. Chromium is mined as chromite (FeCr2O4) ore, with South Africa producing about two-fifths of the world's chromite ores and concentrates. Other significant producers include Kazakhstan, India, Russia, and Turkey. Untapped chromite deposits are abundant but geographically concentrated in Kazakhstan and southern Africa. Native chromium deposits are rare, but some have been discovered, such as in the Udachnaya Mine in Russia, which is a kimberlite pipe rich in diamonds. The reducing environment in this mine facilitated the formation of both elemental chromium and diamonds. Commercially, chromium is obtained by heating chromite ore in the presence of aluminum or silicon. Chromium belongs to the transition metals group (Group 6) and has an electronic configuration of 4s1 3d5 in its neutral state due to the stability of the high-spin configuration. Chromium exhibits a wide range of oxidation states, with +2, +3, and +6 being the most common. The +3 state is the most stable, while +1, +4, and +5 are rare. Compounds of chromium in the +6 oxidation state are strong oxidizing agents. Chromium is passivated by oxygen, forming a thin, protective oxide surface layer that prevents further oxidation. This layer is dense and prevents oxygen diffusion into the underlying material, unlike in plain carbon steels. Chromium is often plated over a nickel layer, which may or may not have been copper-plated first. Unlike many metals such as iron and nickel, chromium does not suffer from hydrogen embrittlement but is susceptible to nitrogen embrittlement, which has prevented the development of straight chromium alloys. Potassium dichromate is a powerful oxidizing agent and is commonly used to clean laboratory glassware of organic residues. It is typically used as a saturated solution in concentrated sulfuric acid. Sodium dichromate is sometimes preferred due to its higher solubility. Chromium(III) oxide (Cr2O3), also known as chrome green, is used in enamel painting and glass staining. Chrome yellow, a brilliant yellow pigment (PbCrO4), is used by painters. Chromic acid (H2CrO4) is a hypothetical compound, but its anions are found in various compounds. Chromium trioxide (CrO3), the acid anhydride of chromic acid, is sold industrially as chromic acid. Chromium is notable for its ability to form quintuple covalent bonds, a property unique to this element. This was achieved using a bulky monodentate ligand that prevents further coordination. Chromium remains the only element for which quintuple bonds have been observed. Chromium has numerous applications. In metallurgy, it is used to impart corrosion resistance and a shiny finish, such as in stainless steel, chrome plating, and anodized aluminum. Chromium compounds are used as dyes and pigments, with chromium(III) oxide serving as a metal polish known as green rouge. Chromium salts color glass emerald green and are responsible for the red color of rubies, including synthetic rubies. Chromium compounds also produce brilliant yellow pigments for painting. Chromium is used as a catalyst, in molds for firing bricks, and in the tanning of leather. Potassium dichromate is a chemical reagent used for cleaning laboratory glassware and as a titrating agent. Chromium(IV) oxide (CrO2) is used in the manufacture of magnetic tape due to its superior performance compared to iron oxide tapes. Chromium compounds are also used in well-drilling muds as anti-corrosive agents, in medicine as dietary supplements (e.g., chromium(III) chloride or chromium(III) picolinate), and in the production of synthetic rubies. Chromium hexacarbonyl (Cr(CO)6) is used as a gasoline additive, and chromium boride (CrB) serves as a high-temperature electrical conductor. Chromium(III) sulfate (Cr2(SO4)3) is used as a green pigment in paints, ceramics, varnishes, and inks, as well as in chrome plating. Chromium(VI) is used in the preparation of gravure printing cylinders to increase their longevity. Biologically, trivalent chromium (Cr(III)) is required in trace amounts for sugar metabolism in humans, as part of the Glucose Tolerance Factor. A deficiency in chromium can lead to a condition known as chromium deficiency. In contrast, hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) is highly toxic and mutagenic when inhaled, as highlighted in the film Erin Brockovich. While Cr(VI) has not been established as a carcinogen when not inhaled, it is a known cause of allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) in solution. Recent studies have shown that chromium picolinate, a popular dietary supplement, can cause chromosomal damage in hamster cells. In the United States, dietary guidelines for daily chromium intake have been reduced to 35 µg for adult males and 25 µg for adult females. Chromium has four stable isotopes, with 52Cr being the most abundant. It also has several radioactive isotopes, most of which have half-lives of less than 24 hours. The isotope 53Cr is the radiogenic decay product of 53Mn and has applications in isotope geology. Variations in 53Cr/52Cr and Mn/Cr ratios in meteorites provide evidence for nucleosynthetic processes that occurred before the formation of the solar system. Chromium metal and chromium(III) compounds are generally not considered health hazards and are essential trace minerals. However, hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) compounds are toxic if ingested or inhaled. The lethal dose of Cr(VI) compounds is approximately half a teaspoon. Most Cr(VI) compounds are irritants to the eyes, skin, and mucous membranes, and chronic exposure can cause permanent eye injury if not properly treated. Cr(VI) is an established human carcinogen. The release of hexavalent chromium into drinking water was the subject of the film Erin Brockovich. Cr(VI) is also one of the substances restricted by the European Restriction of Hazardous Substances Directive. Chromium compounds, previously used in dyes, paints, and leather tanning, are often found in soil and groundwater at abandoned industrial sites, requiring environmental cleanup and remediation. Primer paints containing Cr(VI) are still widely used in aerospace and automobile refinishing applications.
